title: Their 'cannot' means: lacks proximate and complete power
source_text: X. Porro quod docent illi Theologi ne unum quidem bonum opus ab homine post lapsum posse fieri, absque ejusmodi Dei auxilio efficaci voluntatem ad bonum flectente & determinante, intelligunt de potentia proxima & completa: nec aliud per hoc significatum volunt, quam hominem non esse proxime & complete potentem ad bonum aliquod opus faciendum, quamdiu abest gratia efficax, ad illud propter voluntatis morbum & languorem necessaria. Cum enim gratia haec per se efficax simul det velle & posse proximum & completissimum, quicunque hanc gratiam non habet, is non habet velle & posse proximum quod illa largitur.
pass_a_gloss: X. Further what those Theologians teach that not even one good work can be done by man after the fall, without such efficacious help of God bending and determining the will to good, they understand of proximate and complete power: nor do they wish anything else to be signified by this, than that man is not proximately and completely able to do some good work, as long as efficacious grace is absent, necessary for it because of the disease and languor of the will. For since this grace efficacious by itself gives at once willing and proximate and most complete being able, whoever does not have this grace, he does not have the willing and proximate being able which it bestows.
pass_b_english: Thesis X. These theologians teach that after the fall a person cannot perform even one good work without such efficacious aid from God bending and determining the will toward the good. They mean this of proximate and complete power. All they intend is that, so long as the efficacious grace that a sick and listless will needs for a given good work is missing, a person is not proximately and completely able to do it.
Since this grace, efficacious of itself, grants both the willing and the proximate and fullest ability together, anyone without it lacks the willing and the proximate ability that it supplies.
